channel.title: HumanAIBrief · 人-AI 行为
channel.description: 人与 AI、机器人及算法系统交互中的信任、采纳、依赖、归因与决策行为研究

item.title: Teacher self-efficacy in Teacher-AI collaboration: a systematic review
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Although research on Teacher Self-efficacy in Teacher-AI collaboration (TSE-AI) has increased significantly in recent years, no systematic literature synthesis or theoretical integration yet exists. Following PRISMA guidelines and using a thematic synthesis approach, this review examined 59 eligible studies from five databases to clarify how TSE-AI is conceptualized and operationalized across educational levels and AI application scenarios, and to identify its roles as antecedent, mediator, and outcome. The review identified three instrument types, most grounded in Bandura’s social cognitive theory: adapted Teacher Efficacy Scales, domain-specific AI self-efficacy scales, such as the Teacher Artificial Intelligence Competence Self-Efficacy (TAICS) scale, and technology self-efficacy scales. To date, none have been validated as a standard reference, reflecting heterogeneity in measurement approaches. Building on this body of work, the review systematically mapped the paths linking TSE-AI to teachers’psychological and behavioral variables. The construct is conceptualized not as a static trait but as a dynamic, context-sensitive integration of operational and pedagogical efficacy, centered on teachers’beliefs in critically evaluating AI outputs and engaging in joint pedagogical decision-making. This review identified a bidirectional relationship between TSE-AI and Teacher-AI collaboration, the impact of which depends on efficacy calibration: appropriately calibrated efficacy ensures that these beliefs translate into effective collaboration, while exaggerated efficacy may lead to overreliance, potentially undermining teachers’ core instructional and classroom management skills. Directions for future research are discussed.

item.title: Academic writing self-efficacy and AI dependency among university students: academic anxiety as a mediator and teacher emotional support as a moderator
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative AI has become increasingly integrated into university students’ academic writing, offering substantial support while also raising concerns about excessive reliance on AI. Understanding how support within the teaching environment relates to this reliance may help inform educational efforts to address AI dependency. This study examined the psychological and environmental factors associated with AI dependency in academic writing, focusing on academic writing self-efficacy, academic anxiety, and teacher emotional support. Methods Using cross-sectional survey data from 1,012 university students across four regions of China, mediation and moderated mediation effects were tested through structural equation modeling. Results The results showed that lower academic writing self-efficacy was associated with greater AI dependency both directly and indirectly through higher academic anxiety. Although teacher emotional support was negatively correlated with academic anxiety overall, its conditional association with anxiety varied across levels of academic writing self-efficacy: it was negative at lower levels but positive at higher levels. The negative conditional indirect association between academic writing self-efficacy and AI dependency through academic anxiety was also weaker at higher levels of teacher emotional support. Discussion These findings suggest that academic anxiety may help explain the association between academic writing self-efficacy and AI dependency and highlight a potential compensatory role of teacher emotional support among students with lower writing self-efficacy. They underscore the value of considering both students’ writing self-efficacy and support within the teaching environment when developing educational approaches to address excessive reliance on AI in academic writing.

item.title: Social Influence in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Preference for Humans Does Not Deter Artificial Intelligence Influence
item.description:
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a source of social influence. But people often prefer human over AI sources (algorithm aversion/preference for humans), which might prevent AI from influencing humans. However, we outline a theoretical framework that suggests that preferences do not play a causal role in influence. To test this framework, we investigated under which conditions preferences predict AI influence. Participants (N = 1,254) indicated their adviser preference and then made incentivised decisions while receiving advice from AI or human advisers. Participants preferred human over AI advisers but were influenced by AI and humans similarly. A strong aversion to AI advisers had no (Study 1) or a trivial relation (Study 2 and 3) with AI influence, which was explained by confounding variables. When manipulated, preferences did not predict advice-taking, but adviser trustworthiness and competence did (Study 3). Our results suggest that for predicting AI influence, understanding domain-specific social cognitions, not preferences, is critical.

item.title: Artificial intelligence adoption and occupational well-being in higher education management: evidence from universities in Guangzhou
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Universities are increasingly introducing artificial intelligence (AI) tools into administrative and managerial work. Yet evidence on how AI adoption relates to occupational well-being in higher education management remains fragmented. Building on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and contemporary technostress scholarship, this study examines direct, indirect, and conditional associations between AI adoption and occupational well-being in university management in Guangzhou. Methods The cross-sectional questionnaire dataset contained 320 complete records and was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), with a two-stage interaction specification and 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results AI adoption was positively associated with technostress, which was negatively associated with occupational well-being. Neither the direct AI adoption-well-being association nor the conditional total association at mean organizational support was statistically significant. The negative indirect association through technostress was significant at that support level. Perceived organizational support was positively associated with well-being and with a weaker negative technostress-well-being association. The model explained 23.04% of technostress variance and 10.69% of well-being variance. Discussion These results support a statistical stress pathway but do not establish a direct well-being benefit of AI adoption. Cross-sectional associations do not establish causal mechanisms. The study contributes an occupational well-being perspective to AI-enabled university administration and identifies training, workload redesign, and organizational support as priorities for future evaluation.

item.title: Speech-Based Explainable AI for Deception Detection: Insights into Trust Calibration and Mis-calibration
item.description:
ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in complex decision-making tasks across various domains. However, trust mis-calibration in AI, manifested as either over-trust or under-trust, remains a significant challenge, impacting human-AI collaboration and decision quality. This paper investigates factors influencing trust mis-calibration in AI through a user study on a speech-based deception detection task, an inherently complex and ambiguous domain. It examines (1) the relationship between user performance and trust calibration; (2) the role of local explanations (i.e., linguistic and acoustic features of deceptive speech) in shaping trust calibration; and (3) the influence of case-specific cues on trust calibration. In a study involving 52 participants, findings suggest that high-performing users exhibit significantly lower under-trust, but do not differ in over-trust compared to low-performing users. Analysis of local explanations reveals that under-trust occurs when linguistic and acoustic features misalign with deception outcomes. On the other side, over-trust arises when these features align with deception but the AI’s decision does not, suggesting that over-trust follows less rational decision-making patterns. Furthermore, users rely on different cues depending on their trust calibration: under-trusting users focus on speech features, over-trusting users rely on general perception, and properly calibrated users incorporate social, cultural, and emotional cues. These findings underscore the need for AI systems to tailor explanations based on user expertise and develop cognitive strategies to mitigate trust mis-calibration and foster effective human-AI collaboration.

item.title: Antecedents of AI adoption in firm innovation and their association with innovation performance
item.description:
Behaviour and Information Technology
In today’s changing business environment, adopting artificial intelligence (AI) has become a strategy for improving innovation performance. Drawing on the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework and resource orchestration theory (ROT), this study combines structural equation modelling (SEM), fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), and propensity score matching (PSM) to examine AI adoption configurations and their associations with innovation performance. Using data from 205 Chinese firms, the study finds that technological factors (infrastructure and relative advantage), organisational factors (top management support and professional expertise), and environmental factors (competitive pressure and government support) are positively associated with AI adoption. The SEM results also reveal mediating and moderating relationships among the examined factors. The fsQCA results identify high AI adoption configurations: external resource compensation (C1), internal resource activation (C2), and internal-external resource integration (C3). The PSM results show that firms adopting AI through C2 and C3 exhibit significantly higher innovation performance than matched firms that do not fit any of the three high AI adoption configurations, whereas C1 shows no statistically significant association with innovation performance. By identifying AI adoption configurations and their patterns of association with innovation performance, this study provides practical insights into how firms can tailor AI adoption strategies to their resource endowments.

item.title: Too good to resist? Affective engagement and a competence–regulation gap predict self-reported over-reliance on generative AI among vocational foreign-language learners
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been adopted by students faster than nearly any earlier educational technology, yet over-reliance remains underexamined precisely among the learners inspiring that concern. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study identified predictors of self-reported over-reliance among foreign-language majors ( n = 249) at a Chinese higher vocational college. Quantitative findings revealed two patterns. First, affective factors dominated: fear of missing out ( β = 0.50) and anthropomorphic attachment ( β = 0.27) were the strongest predictors, whereas neither self-regulated learning nor perceived AI literacy was related to over-reliance on its own ( r = −0.03 and 0.08, both ns). Because these two overlap substantially ( r = 0.67), the opposite-signed coefficients they take in the model cannot be interpreted in isolation. What mattered instead was their gap: the discrepancy between feeling AI-literate and reporting that one regulates one’s own learning predicted over-reliance ( β = 0.21), persisting even under controls for acquiescent responding. Second, person-centered and configurational analyses agreed: learners low in affective engagement reported the least over-reliance ( M = 3.19). A profile elevated on every indicator did not survive scrutiny for response bias, and fear of missing out combined with anthropomorphic attachment was consistently associated with over-reliance regardless of self-rated competence. Interviews with five learners suggested candidate explanations. Humanlike warmth lowered the psychological cost of delegation. Fear of falling behind, normalized by peers, gradually eroded personal standards through repeated choices. Perceived competence enabled over-reliance rather than restraining it, interrupted only by enacted self-regulation. The emotional relationship formed with the tool tracked over-reliance more closely than learners’ own competence assessment.

item.title: When User Requests are Ambiguous: The Role of Response Explainability in Shaping User Experience with LLM-Based Smart Home Assistants
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into smart home assistants (SHAs), voice interactions are moving beyond constrained commands toward open-ended conversations, increasing ambiguity in user requests. Therefore, this study investigates how request ambiguity and response explainability affect users’ perceived trust, satisfaction, and pleasure in the context of LLM-based smart home assistant (SHA). A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 211 participants across three scenarios: device control, information inquiry, and schedule planning. Results showed that request ambiguity negatively affected all three outcomes under low explainability. LLM response explainability substantially improved users’ evaluations of trust, satisfaction, and pleasure under high ambiguity, mitigating the negative effects by clarifying how the assistant interpreted user intent and why it generated a particular response. These findings advance understanding of ambiguity and explainability in human–AI interaction from a user experience perspective and highlight the importance of adaptive explanation strategies in LLM-based SHAs.

item.title: Judging AI, Distancing the Self: Warmth, Competence, and Third-Person Perception of AI Influence
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Drawing on the stereotype content model and third-person perception (TPP) theory, this study examines how warmth and competence perceptions of generative AI shape negative attitudes toward the technology and biased judgments that others are more vulnerable to AI influence than oneself. Conducting an online survey (N = 1273), the study reveals that both warmth and competence were associated with lower negative attitudes toward generative AI, with warmth showing the stronger association. Moreover, negative attitudes were positively associated with TPP. AI efficacy was found to strengthen the effect of competence, but not warmth, on negative attitudes. These findings have implications for human-AI interaction design by revealing that AI-based conversational agents can potentially reduce AI fear by conveying warmth alongside calibrated competence and that AI interface and literacy efforts should address users’ self-other bias to support more accurate appraisals of AI effects.

item.title: Social use of generative artificial intelligence and college emerging adults’ socioemotional well-being: a dual-motive approach
item.description:
Behaviour and Information Technology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is quickly integrated into youth’s daily lives, including their navigation and management of social relationships. The study focuses on college emerging adults’ social use of GenAI, defined as using AI for social purposes. Informed by the Multidimensional Model of Social Media Use, we distinguish between the social enhancement and compensation motives. Survey data from 497 college emerging adults (Mage = 21.58, SD = 2.97) revealed that the social enhancement motive had a more dynamic relationship with socioemotional well-being, associated with higher social competence but also stronger AI attachment; the social compensation motive was related to poorer well-being, associated with lower social competence, greater loneliness, and stronger AI attachment. Dysregulated engagement was the most salient mechanism, followed by intimate self-disclosure to AI. Critical evaluation and contextualised application of AI did not mediate the paths between the motives and well-being. The dual-motive model provides a useful framework to examine AI’s roles in youth’s social development, and identifies dysregulated engagement and intimate self-disclosure as viable targets for intervention.

item.title: Accuracy- versus efficiency-driven artificial intelligence use: Purpose matters, yet user dehumanization persists.
item.description:
Technology Mind and Behavior
Building on prior studies that have documented the dehumanization of the users of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, that is, the tendency for observers to attribute less humanness to individuals who use AI than to those who do not, the present research examines whether and how different AI use purposes (i.e., accuracy- vs. efficiency-driven use) influence this effect. We conducted four preregistered studies (total N = 1,270) spanning diverse professional domains. We observed that accuracy-driven AI use negatively predicted the dehumanization of AI users, whereas efficiency-driven AI use positively predicted such dehumanization (Study 1). Furthermore, accuracy-driven AI users elicited less dehumanization than their efficiency-driven counterparts did, a pattern that proved robust across both intuitive assessments of dehumanization (Study 2) and deliberative ratings of humanness traits (Studies 3 and 4). However, both accuracy- and efficiency-driven AI users were significantly dehumanized compared with non-AI users (Study 4), demonstrating that while purpose matters, AI user dehumanization persists. These findings extend the literature on the social cost of AI and offer novel insights into how human–AI interaction shapes interpersonal dynamics .

item.title: Students’ intention to engage with hypothetical AI-recommended ESG campaigns: Integrating TPB and UTAUT via perceived AI competence and trust in AI
item.description:
Computers in Human Behavior Reports
As digital platforms increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) to curate content, university students may encounter environmental, social, and governance (ESG) campaigns through algorithmic recommendation systems. This study examined students’ perceptions and stated intention to engage with AI-recommended ESG campaigns within a standardized hypothetical scenario. Participants were not exposed to an operational AI recommendation system, and actual ESG participation was not measured. The study integrated the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) with selected UTAUT antecedents and two AI-specific constructs: perceived AI competence and trust in AI. Survey data were collected from undergraduate students at one Vietnamese university (N = 218), with 199 valid responses retained after screening and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Performance expectancy and effort expectancy were positively associated with perceived AI competence, which was positively associated with trust in AI. Trust in AI was positively associated with attitude, while attitude showed the largest standardized association with engagement intention. Perceived behavioral control was also positively associated with intention, whereas subjective norm was not significant. Bootstrapped indirect effects were consistent with sequential associations linking technology-related beliefs to intention through perceived AI competence, trust in AI, and attitude. Academic year positively moderated the performance expectancy–competence association (β = 0.112, p = .027), such that this association was stronger in higher academic years; the effort expectancy–competence interaction was not statistically significant. These findings concern perceptions and stated behavioral intentions within a hypothetical scenario and should not be interpreted as evidence of actual AI exposure or ESG participation.

item.title: The effect of response typing speed on trust in AI chat interfaces
item.description:
Computers in Human Behavior Reports
Trust in artificial intelligence systems has become increasingly important as these systems assume advisory and decision-support roles. The present studies examine whether the temporal presentation of artificial intelligence (AI) generated responses, specifically typing animation speed, affects trust in chat-based interfaces. In Experiment 1, participants ( N = 71) interacted with three AI agents using pre-scripted question-response pairs detailing different facts about exotic animals. Response presentation speed (slow, fast, or instant) was manipulated within subjects. Results showed that compared to instant presentation, typing animations significantly increased trust in the AI agent but not trust in individual responses. Experiment 2 ( N = 68) employed similar procedures but used a live language model and allowed participants to generate their own questions. Under these more naturalistic conditions, presentation speed influenced both measures of trust, with typing animations consistently producing higher trust than instant presentation. These findings demonstrate that temporal presentation features can systematically shape trust judgments independent of content quality.

item.title: Latent profile analysis of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates: associations with positive acceptance and striving
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background The rapid integration of generative AI tools into higher education has raised concerns about problematic AI dependence and its links to academic procrastination, yet little is known about how these phenomena co-occur at the individual level among medical undergraduates. Objective This study identified latent profiles of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates, examined correlates of profile membership, and tested how profiles differ in positive acceptance and striving. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 530 undergraduates at two Chinese medical universities (March–May 2026). Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed on seven dimension sum scores from the AIDep-22 and the Academic Procrastination Scale. Multinomial logistic regression examined demographic and AI-use correlates of profile membership, and the BCH approach compared positive acceptance and striving across profiles. Results A three-profile solution best fit the data: Class 1, “low dependence–low procrastination” (41.1%); Class 2, “high dependence–high procrastination” (25.8%); and Class 3, “functional/cognitive reliance–low procrastination” (33.0%). Relative to Class 1, membership in Class 3 was associated with first-choice major enrollment (OR for non-first-choice = 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.75), higher subjective AI familiarity (OR for low vs. high familiarity = 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74) and more frequent AI use (OR for often vs. always = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68); only AI use frequency distinguished Class 2 from Class 1 (OR for often vs. always = 0.25, 95% CI 0.15–0.42). Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p < 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. Targeted support should prioritize the latter rather than treating all frequent AI users as uniformly at risk.

item.title: Production-source disclosures, higher-order creative attributions, and audience reception of two-dimensional animation: evidence from a randomized source-disclosure experiment
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Attribution theory explains how audiences use observable information to infer otherwise unobservable agents and processes behind creative work. This study applied this perspective to examine how production-source disclosures influence source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience reception of two-dimensional animation. Methods In a randomized experiment, 626 adults were assigned to one of four production-source disclosure conditions—undisclosed, human-made, human–AI collaborative, or AI-led—while viewing the same three animation clips, all of which were actually produced through human–AI collaboration. We examined between-condition differences in source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience-reception outcomes, as well as concurrent associations between higher-order creative attributions and audience reception. Results The disclosures clearly differentiated participants’ perceptions of AI and human involvement. Perceived creative effort was statistically significant before correction but did not meet the α = 0.05 criterion after Holm adjustment ( p = 0.0502); the only corrected contrast indicated lower perceived creative effort in the human–AI collaborative condition than in the human-made condition. No statistically reliable omnibus between-condition differences emerged for perceived authorship, perceived emotional authenticity, artistic evaluation, situational immersion, or viewing and recommendation intention. Higher-order creative attributions were positively associated with all three audience-reception indicators in concurrent analyses, although the strong correlation between perceived emotional authenticity and situational immersion warrants caution about measurement overlap. Discussion The findings indicate that the diagnosticity of a production-source cue depends on the judgment target: the disclosures clearly reorganized perceived production roles but did not yield statistically reliable corresponding differences across most higher-order creative attributions or reception outcomes. The attribution–reception relations represent concurrent covariation rather than causal mediation. Because the three clips were presented in a fixed order, material and order effects cannot be separated, and the equivalence analyses did not establish negligible between-condition differences.

item.title: Working With Robots: How Robot Proportion in Human-Robot Teams and Robot Anthropomorphism Shape Employee Turnover Intention
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Although robots are increasingly reshaping organizational workflows, how the robot proportion in human-robot teams affects employees’ turnover intention remains underexplored. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we examine whether, why, and when robot proportion exerts divergent effects on turnover intention through two pathways: resource gain and resource loss. Evidence from a scenario-based experiment (Study 1, N = 290) and a three-wave field study (Study 2, N = 306) reveals that these two pathways operate in opposing directions. Specifically, work goal progress and work loneliness mediate the relationship between robot proportion in human-robot teams and turnover intention. Robot anthropomorphism further moderates these pathways: higher anthropomorphism strengthens the beneficial effect on work goal progress, whereas lower anthropomorphism amplifies the detrimental effect on work loneliness. This study offers initial evidence on how the structural composition of human-robot teams shapes employees’ turnover intention, and it provides practical implications for organizations deploying robotic coworkers.

item.title: Artificial intelligence and teacher self-efficacy: from technology adoption to AI-mediated efficacy reconstruction
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in educational practice, transforming lesson planning, instructional delivery, assessment, learning analytics, and teacher professional development. Although research on AI in education has expanded rapidly, the psychological consequences of AI adoption for teachers remain theoretically fragmented. Existing studies have examined technology acceptance, AI literacy, technology self-efficacy, instructional confidence, and professional identity, yet these constructs have rarely been integrated into a coherent account of how AI reshapes teachers’ beliefs about their own professional capabilities. This narrative review synthesizes the emerging literature through a theory-building perspective grounded primarily in social cognitive theory and informed by technology acceptance, cognitive load, professional identity, social comparison, and human–AI interaction perspectives. We propose a framework of AI-Mediated Efficacy Reconstruction, conceptualizing AI not as a direct determinant of teacher self-efficacy but as a socio-technical factor that changes the availability, interpretation, and attribution of efficacy-relevant experiences. AI can facilitate mastery experiences, provide vicarious learning opportunities, offer timely feedback, reduce routine cognitive demands, and expand access to professional learning. However, the same technologies may generate cognitive overload, technical anxiety, professional comparison, identity threat, reduced autonomy, and technological dependence. We identify Efficacy Attribution as a potentially central mechanism determining whether AI-supported performance is internalized as evidence of teachers’ own professional capability or attributed primarily to the technological system. On this basis, we distinguish Augmented Efficacy, in which AI extends teachers’ capabilities while preserving professional agency, from Dependent Efficacy, in which perceived competence becomes increasingly contingent upon AI assistance. The framework further proposes that these processes are moderated by teacher characteristics, AI-system characteristics, teaching tasks, organizational context, and time. We conclude by outlining implications for measurement, teacher professional development, AI design, organizational policy, and future longitudinal and experimental research.

item.title: When AI Performs, What Remains? An Integrative Review of Generative AI and Cognitive Capital in Individuals and Organizations
item.description:
Cyberpsychology Behavior and Social Networking
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive, and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enable an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism, we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

item.title: Generative AI Use and Two-Wave Change in Well-Being and Ill-Being: A Pre- and Post-generative AI Era Panel Study
item.description:
Cyberpsychology Behavior and Social Networking
As generative artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly spreads, concerns about its impact on users' mental health have surged. However, previous studies have yielded contradicting results owing to theoretical and methodological limitations. To address these gaps, this study investigates how generative AI adoption, usage time, and multidimensional AI dependency are related to two-wave changes in subjective well-being (self-esteem and life satisfaction) and ill-being (loneliness, anxiety, and depression). A two-wave longitudinal panel survey of 1,022 South Korean adults was conducted, with data collected in October 2022 (the pre-generative AI era) and March 2026 (the post-generative AI era), providing a prediffusion baseline against which change can be indexed. A multilevel modeling approach was used to examine within-subject and between-subject differences simultaneously. The results revealed that simple AI adoption and daily usage time were largely unrelated to changes in users' subjective well-being or ill-being. However, a problematic form of AI use-specifically, withdrawal-type dependency characterized by psychological distress or frustration when unable to use AI-was associated with less decline in loneliness, with a suggestive but less robust pattern for depression, over time. These findings indicate that the use of generative AI is neither inherently beneficial nor intrinsically harmful. Instead of focusing merely on adoption or usage time, future research and practice should further examine maladaptive withdrawal-type AI dependency as a potential marker of less favorable mental-health change.

item.title: Mitigating Information Manipulation of AI Influencers
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Artificial Intelligence (AI) influencers’ wider adoption makes addressing the risks of perceived information manipulation crucial. This study employs a mixed-methods approach to investigate the antecedents and consequences of perceived information manipulation by AI influencers. Drawing on Hunt-Vitell Theory and Goal-Framing Theory, a theoretical model is tested using survey data from 625 participants in Singapore. The results indicate that reasonable use, privacy protection, non-deception, personal development, and perceived enjoyment significantly reduce perceived information manipulation, while informed consent has a negative but non-significant effect. Perceived information manipulation negatively impacts both routine and infusion use. Thematic analysis of 15 follow-up semi-structured interviews generates meta-inferences that provide both confirmation and complementary insights into the psychological mechanisms underlying the quantitative results. Based on these findings, this study offers practical recommendations for AI influencer operators and policymakers to mitigate potential negative social impacts, enabling the ethical realization of AI influencers’ full potential.

item.title: AI dependence and academic engagement among Chinese university students: a three-wave longitudinal conditional process study of self-efficacy and physical activity
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can support university learning, yet psychological reliance on AI-generated feedback may limit independent mastery experiences. Under an integrated I-PACE–social cognitive framework, this three-wave observational study examined whether self-efficacy for learning and performance statistically accounted for the association between AI dependence and subsequent academic engagement, and whether physical activity moderated the first-stage association. The analysis was based on 1,068 quality-screened students matched across baseline (T1), Week 4 (T2), and Week 8 (T3) questionnaires. AI dependence and physical activity were measured at T1, self-efficacy at T1/T2, and academic engagement at T1/T3. Standardized regression-based PROCESS Models 4 and 7 adjusted for baseline self-efficacy and engagement, demographics, and AI-use intensity. Higher T1 AI dependence was associated with lower T2 self-efficacy ( β = −0.137), while T2 self-efficacy was positively associated with T3 engagement ( β = 0.114). The first-stage interaction was small ( β = 0.073; ΔR 2 = 0.005), with an index of moderated mediation of 0.008 (5,000-resample 95% bootstrap CI [0.002, 0.017]). Inverse-probability-of-completion weighting produced similar core estimates; longitudinal measurement-invariance and latent autoregressive SEM results are additionally reported as sensitivity evidence. The results identify a short-term, temporally ordered indirect association involving academic self-efficacy, not an established causal mechanism. Educators may preserve students’ independent mastery opportunities when designing AI-assisted coursework.

item.title: Distance Does Not Matter: The Role of Physical Robot Presence in Social HRI with Older Adults
item.description:
International Journal of Social Robotics
Abstract As the global older population increases, more older adults need assistance in their daily lives. There is an increasing interest in using social robots to assist with everyday activities to promote overall wellbeing and health. However, whether and how social robot physical presence can influence human-robot interactions (HRI) with older adults has not yet been explored. In this paper, we present the first long-term HRI study conducted in a long-term care home that investigates the interaction behaviors of older adults during dance sessions facilitated by physically present and remotely present social human-like robots. Our results show that the older adults had similarly high levels of engagement and enjoyment during the interactions regardless of if the social robot was physically or remotely present. Although higher participation rates were observed in the in-person HRI, participation rates in the remote HRI were consistent to those in other non-robot facilitated physical activity interventions for older adults. Overall, this paper explores the role of robot presence and its impact on HRI, while providing insight into the potential use of remote HRI for providing social assistance to older adults.

item.title: Design-thinking scaffolds for learner-agency-preserving AI use: effects on creative self-efficacy, cognitive flexibility, and engagement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative AI can facilitate the production of student work but may also displace learners' responsibility for problem framing, evaluation, and revision. This study examined whether design-thinking scaffolds were associated with creative self-efficacy, cognitive flexibility, and problem-solving engagement during AI-supported project learning. Methods A three-condition, four-wave quasi-experimental study included 162 undergraduates in six intact class sections (54 per condition). Non-AI project learning, ordinary GenAI use, and design-thinking-scaffolded GenAI use were compared across a four-week educational design task. Baseline-adjusted models assessed self-reported outcomes, human-coded AI-use logs, and independently rated products from 54 teams. Cluster-bootstrap analyses examined temporally ordered indirect associations and moderation by pre-intervention AI over-reliance. Results Compared with ordinary GenAI, the scaffolded condition showed higher T2 creative self-efficacy (adjusted difference = 0.33, p = 0.006), T3 cognitive flexibility (0.35, p = 0.003), and T4 engagement (0.35, p = 0.004). Mean team product quality was 20.14 in the scaffolded condition, compared with 17.62 under ordinary GenAI and 16.76 without AI. Coded prompts showed fewer answer-completion requests and more comparison, critique, and reflection. Indirect estimates via creative self-efficacy (0.07), cognitive flexibility (0.09), and their sequential pathway (0.04) had bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. Higher initial AI over-reliance weakened the overall engagement contrast and the two single-mediator indirect pathways, whereas the moderated-sequential index had a confidence interval including zero. Discussion The findings are consistent with agency-preserving cognitive offloading when instructional scaffolds retain student responsibility for higher-order decisions. Intact-section allocation, task-specific self-reports, and limited section-level replication preclude strong causal or general-transfer claims.

item.title: AI Versus Human Recommendation: Effects on Decision Switch Under Conflict
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated in everyday decision-making, understanding how individuals respond to AI versus human advice is critical. The present study examined whether individuals are more likely to revise their initial decisions based on recommendations’ source (AI vs. Human) and stance (Agree vs. Disagree), while holding recommendation content constant. Fifty-nine participants completed eight game scenarios from popular casino games. After each initial choice, participants received a recommendation and were prompted to re-make the same decision. Mixed-effects logistic regression revealed that there is a strong tendency for participants to switch their selection when presented with disagreeing recommendations, regardless of its source. No significant differences were found in switching behaviors between AI and human-disagree conditions, though confidence increased in presence of decision switch when the opposing recommendation came from AI. Future research should explore how individual differences and contextual factors influence adoption of AI advice.

item.title: From emotional comfort to relational investment in generative AI companionship: evidence from SEM and fsQCA
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
With the rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI), chatbots are evolving from instrumental assistants into emotionally responsive companions. This study develops a low-friction relational process model to examine the relationships linking generative AI companionship with emotional relief and positive social investment. AI emotional responsiveness, non-judgemental interaction, and memory-based continuity were conceptualized as interaction conditions, while perceived being understood, deep self-disclosure, and synthetic attachment were specified as psychological mechanisms. Structural equation modeling (SEM), bootstrap mediation analysis, moderation analysis, and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) were employed to analyse 765 valid responses from generative AI chatbot users. The SEM results show that non-judgemental interaction exhibits the most consistent pattern of associations with perceived being understood, deep self-disclosure, synthetic attachment, emotional relief, and positive social investment. Perceived being understood and synthetic attachment show relatively stable mediating patterns, whereas deep self-disclosure is significantly associated with emotional relief but shows a less consistent association with positive social investment. Perceived AI safety and self-disclosure habit play differentiated moderating roles. The fsQCA findings reveal three configurations for high emotional relief and four configurations for high positive social investment, complementing the SEM results. This study provides a systematic account of generative AI companionship and offers implications for safer and relationship-oriented AI design.
