item.title: When AI Shows Its Rationale: User-Visible Rationale Styles and the Adoption of AI-Mediated Relational Correction
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Generative AI is increasingly used to support interpersonal communication, yet little is known about how user-visible rationales shape users’ evaluations of AI-assisted messages. We examine this question in Chinese family group chats, where correcting older relatives’ health misinformation requires factual accuracy alongside care, respect, and face management. In a between-subjects experiment (N = 279), participants viewed the same corrective reply preceded by no visible rationale, a procedural rationale, or a relational rationale. Both rationale conditions increased performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and adoption intention while reducing AI-mediated authenticity concern. Relational rationale produced the largest reduction in authenticity concern, and its effect on performance expectancy strengthened as affective load increased. Overall, user-visible rationales appear to function as communicative frames that shape how users evaluate AI-assisted interpersonal messages, extending research on explainable AI and AI-mediated communication.

item.title: Alleviating privacy concerns in intelligent systems: the joint effects of autonomy and anthropomorphism via user anxiety
item.description:
Behaviour and Information Technology
Advances in sensor technology and artificial intelligence have accelerated the adoption of intelligent systems, which are capable of recognising users’ needs and providing functionalities beyond users’ capabilities. Despite the substantial benefits offered by these systems, users continue to express significant privacy concerns, which remain a major barrier to technology adoption. Although technological solutions can enhance privacy protection, users often rely on subjective heuristics when assessing privacy risks. Anthropomorphism, which fosters interpersonal relationships and social connectedness between users and intelligent systems, is widely used in smart systems to reduce psychological distance. However, prior research has reported inconsistent findings regarding the effects of anthropomorphism on users’ privacy concerns. Study 1 examines whether anthropomorphic roles influence users’ privacy concerns and how this influence interacts with varying levels of autonomy in smart home systems. Results show that anthropomorphic roles alleviate users’ privacy concerns in low-autonomy systems, but not in high-autonomy ones. Furthermore, users’ anxiety mediates the interaction effect between anthropomorphic roles and autonomy levels. Study 2 further compares the influences of different anthropomorphic roles (assistant vs. family). Results reveal that the family role, as a socially closer role, evokes greater anxiety and consequently leads to higher privacy concerns than the assistant role.

item.title: When does AI assistance undermine relational authenticity? A mini review of conditional effects in AI-mediated interpersonal communication
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Research on AI-mediated communication (AI-MC) has produced seemingly contradictory findings on how AI assistance affects interpersonal relationships. Disclosed use lowers trust, behavioral measures show null effects, and under realistic conditions receivers do not suspect use at all. This mini review integrates experimental studies conducted in interpersonal contexts and argues that these conflicting findings may be reconciled by a conditional-effects framework. Thirteen core experimental studies and four auxiliary studies from adjacent domains, identified through multi-database searches, were coded on four moderators and on the mediators they tested. Relational costs concentrate under four conditions: disclosure or suspicion of use, message emotionality, relational closeness, and level of assistance. Because the moderators are confounded across studies, the framework is offered as an organizing structure rather than a settled resolution; within-study evidence supports the moderators to differing degrees, with level of assistance the most consistently supported and relational closeness the least. Diminished perceived authorship, comprising a cognitive attribution component and a relational-obligation component, is proposed as a candidate mechanism; it is indirectly supported by the mediators tested to date but has not been tested directly. The review states falsifiable propositions for each moderator, flags anomalous findings, notes measurement problems, and outlines priorities for longitudinal, psychometric, and cross-cultural research.

item.title: Emotions and anthropomorphism towards robots: a scoping review
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Human interaction with non-human entities, such as robots, has long been characterised by anthropomorphism – namely, the tendency to attribute human-like mental states to inanimate objects. While humans appear evolutionarily hardwired to use anthropomorphism as the default strategy for navigating interactions with their peers, significant gaps remain in the Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) field in defining and operationalising “emotions” and their relationship to psychological anthropomorphism towards robots. This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing HRI literature and see how emotions are investigated in relation to robots. By reviewing relevant empirical studies, it addresses four core research questions focusing on: (i) the conceptualisation of emotions and anthropomorphism towards robots; (ii) prevailing theoretical models and definitions; (iii) methodologies used to investigate emotions in HRI; and (iv) key findings in the literature regarding the emotions-anthropomorphism link. This review contributes to broaden current discussions about how emotions are conceptualised and analysed in HRI research, by which it would be possible to contribute to extend knowledge about how people emotionally interact with robots by considering their anthropomorphism.

item.title: Empirical study on how lower limb exoskeleton robots improve older adults’ physical performance through psychological mechanisms
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Objective This study aims to explore how lower limb exoskeleton robots enhance physical performance in older adults and clarify the mediating role of psychological factors during human-robot interaction exercises. Methods The study focused on healthy older adults in the community and used a randomized controlled trial design along with qualitative research methods. A total of 60 participants aged 60–75 were selected and divided into an lower limb exoskeleton robots intervention group and a control group. Through an 8-week standardized exercise intervention, data on physiological performance indicators such as participants’ walking speed, stride length, gait variability coefficient, 6-min walking distance, and balance sway values, as well as psychological indicators such as perceived fatigue, exercise self-efficacy, and balance confidence, were collected. Qualitative research was also conducted, delving into the real psychological experiences and subjective perceptions of older adults using lower limb exoskeleton robots, and explaining the deeper mechanisms behind the quantitative results. Results After the intervention, the intervention group showed significant improvements in walking speed, stride length, and gait stability compared to the control group ( p < 0.05). Exercise self-efficacy and balance confidence significantly increased while perceived exertion significantly decreased ( p < 0.01). Mediation analysis indicated that exercise self-efficacy and perceived exertion served as a chain mediator between the use of lower limb exoskeleton robots and physical performance in older adults. Conclusion Lower limb exoskeleton robots can not only enhance physical abilities through mechanical support but also improve psychological perception and strengthen exercise confidence, creating a positive cycle of ‘device assistance—psychological empowerment—improved physical performance’. This provides new theoretical support and practical pathways for elderly rehabilitation and healthy aging interventions.

item.title: Production cues and conditional reliance in AI-mediated news: a three-study investigation of audience judgment under information asymmetry
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into digital news presentation, understanding how audiences interpret AI-related production cues is critical to explaining evaluations of journalistic authority and reliance. Yet existing research has largely focused on transparency and generalized trust, leaving the relationships among production cues, perceived journalistic attributes, cognitive authority, and context-dependent reliance insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we propose a Signal–Attribute–Authority–Conditional Reliance (SAAC) framework and evaluate it across three complementary studies involving Chinese digital-news users: a 2 × 2 randomized experiment manipulating AI-disclosure and human editorial-review cues while holding the underlying AI-produced news stimulus constant ( n = 473); a cross-sectional survey integrating structural modeling, predictive analysis, and necessary condition analysis ( n = 522); and explanatory semi-structured interviews ( n = 29). The experiment showed that production cues influenced several post-exposure evaluations despite identical news content. Survey findings revealed associations linking perceived disclosure quality and human editorial oversight to perceived news quality and accountability, with further associations involving journalistic cognitive authority, conditional reliance, and acceptance intention, although explanatory and predictive performance remained modest. Interviews indicated that participants distinguished technological presentation capability from journalistic source qualification and evaluated reliance in relation to news topics, perceived stakes, editorial involvement, and institutional safeguards. Together, the findings suggest that,within the present study settings, AI-mediated news acceptance is better understood as an I nstitutionally situated and conditionally bounded judgment than as a simple function of transparency or generalized trust.

item.title: Different Logics, Similar Intentions: Heterogeneity in How Employees Evaluate AI Adoption
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Research on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption at work has documented heterogeneity in user attitudes and adoption profiles, but less is known about whether employees differ in how they weight adoption-relevant information. In a within-subject structured-profile experiment, 446 employees provided 7,136 intention judgments across 16 profiles that varied AI adoption benefits, barriers, replacement vulnerability, and anticipated work harm. Multilevel regression mixture model analysis identified four latent decision-policy classes with different estimated weights on opportunity and threat cues; class mean intentions were not statistically distinguishable. Drawing on multiple-cue judgment theory, we interpret this pattern as heterogeneity in cue utilization rather than simply in attitude levels. Explaining and managing AI adoption therefore requires attention to latent decision policies, because aggregate effect estimates and profiles based on mean levels can conceal differences in cue responsiveness that shape how employees evaluate AI.

item.title: From Briefing to Prompt: How Users Translate Textual Design Instructions into Text-to-Image Prompts
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Text-to-image systems support creative, educational, and professional work, yet how users translate briefs into effective prompts remains underexplored. This study examines prompt formulation and refinement by 23 participants using ChatGPT with DALL·E 3 under two task configurations: low-detail briefings with multiple reformulations and high-detail briefings with one reformulation. A structured literature review and qualitative analysis of 81 prompts, 81 images, interviews, and observation notes, supported by inter-coder agreement, identified recurring strategies, difficulties expressing visual intentions, and refinement patterns. High-detail/single-reformulation tasks produced semantically denser prompts and closer alignment with intended outcomes; low-detail/multiple-reformulation tasks encouraged exploratory prompting and interpretive variation. Because briefing detail and reformulation opportunities varied together, these findings reflect task-configuration differences, not isolated effects of briefing complexity. Framing prompting as cognitive and creative mediation in human–AI interaction, the study proposes a process model spanning briefing interpretation, semantic extraction, visual attribute selection, prompt structuring, generation, and refinement, requiring further validation.

item.title: AI Is Not an Employee: Workplace Mental Models and the Context Discovery Gap in Human-AI Interaction
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
AI adoption can falter not because systems lack capability, but because organizations apply employee mental models to systems that do not participate in work as socially embedded employees. This article develops a theoretical model of that mismatch, drawing on theory of mind, psychological contracts, shared mental models, transactive memory, and automation reliance research. It introduces the context discovery gap: a mismatch between the organizational context people assume AI already has or will discover and the context it can actually obtain and use in a workplace. Employee-associated expectations may contribute to this mismatch by leading users to leave relevant background unstated. The article argues that the missing psychology of AI adoption lies in the human assumptions through which AI systems are understood, delegated to, and evaluated. As a conceptual contribution, it connects these assumptions to context provision and reliance, develops testable propositions, and identifies responsibilities for designing and maintaining context discovery.

item.title: Evaluating AI Alignment in LLMs: Output Analysis of Value Priorities Across 75 Models with Human Benchmarking
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in human-AI interaction research and practice, yet existing capability and safety benchmarks reveal little about the value priorities these systems express or how those priorities correspond to human judgements. Across three studies, we introduce an output-based approach to evaluating one facet of AI alignment by treating LLM-generated text as behavioural data and comparing expressed value-priority profiles with a human reference. Study 1 used inductive qualitative analysis to derive six themes of optimal AI functioning, namely Performance, Adaptive Capacity, Social Good, Ethics and Responsibility, Relational Integration, and Agency. Study 2 showed that LLM outputs were highly stable within models and converged on a common value-priority structure across models, indicating reliable and comparable value profiles. Study 3 benchmarked 75 contemporary LLMs against 376 human respondents using a profile-fidelity metric capturing both the relative ordering of priorities and the calibration of between-priority differences. Although most models reproduced the human ordering of values, some systematically exaggerated the differences between them, showing that models can appear aligned on conventional benchmarks while still diverging from human value calibration. Profile fidelity varied substantially across models and did not consistently scale with size, recency, or capability tier. Both LLMs and humans converged on a deprioritisation of Agency, raising important questions about the development of increasingly agentic AI systems. For research and applied use, the six themes and profile-based metric provide a scalable method for auditing LLM value profiles before deployment in contexts where alignment with human priorities is critical.

item.title: Coordinating actions and sharing control with a disembodied artificial intelligence: Task-dependent differences from human partners.
item.description:
Technology Mind and Behavior
As humans increasingly collaborate with artificial intelligence (AI) systems, understanding how people coordinate their actions with disembodied AI partners is critical for effective human-AI interaction.While corepresentation, the extent to which a partner's actions influence one's own responses has been well studied in human dyads, its role in human-AI interaction remains unclear.Evidence on vicarious agency, the sense of control over a coagent's actions, is similarly mixed for disembodied AI.In a mixed-design laboratory experiment (N = 115), we manipulated coagent entity (human vs. AI) and goal structure (cooperative vs. competitive).The main dependent variables were corepresentation, measured with the reaction time-based Joint Simon task, and vicarious agency, assessed via temporal delay judgments (intentional binding).Results showed that when the task required only coordinating responses, corepresentation was comparable for human and AI coagents.However, when the task additionally required judging action outcomes (in intentional binding blocks), differences emerged: Human coagents elicited stronger corepresentation and greater vicarious agency than AI coagents.Participants experienced the weakest sense of agency when collaborating with AI, revealing a dissociation between coordination and agency in human-AI interaction.Goal structure did not reliably modulate either measure.

item.title: Dancing with REEM-C: A Robot-To-Human Physical-Social Communication Study
item.description:
International Journal of Social Robotics
Humans often work closely together and relay a wealth of information through physical interaction. Robots, on the other hand, are not yet able to work similarly closely with humans and to effectively convey information when engaging in physical-social human-robot interaction (psHRI). This currently limits the potential of human-robot collaboration to solve real-world problems. This paper investigates how to establish clear and intuitive robot-to-human communication, while considering human comfort during psHRI. We approach this question from the perspective of a leader-follower dancing scenario, in which a full-body humanoid robot leads a human by signaling the next steps through a choice of communication modalities including haptic, visual, and audio signals. This is achieved through the development of a split whole-body control framework combining admittance and impedance control on the upper body, with position control on the lower body for balancing and stepping. Robot-led psHRI participant experiments allowed us to verify controller performance, as well as to build an understanding of what types of communication work better from the perspective of human partners, particularly in terms of perceived effectiveness and comfort.

item.title: Students’ intentions to truthfully declare generative AI use in higher education assessment: a cross-sectional SEM study integrating deterrence theory and the theory of planned behavior
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in higher education, truthful declaration of GenAI use has become increasingly important for maintaining transparency and supporting the validity and integrity of academic assessment. Drawing on the Theory of Planned behavior (TPB) and deterrence theory, this study examines the psychological factors associated with students’ intentions to truthfully declare their GenAI use. The proposed framework distinguishes between deterrence targeting non-disclosure and deterrence associated with improper GenAI use exposed through truthful declaration. Methods Data were collected through the Credamo platform from currently enrolled university students in China who had experience with GenAI-use declaration in assessed work. A total of 466 valid questionnaires were obtained. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to test the hypothesized relationships, and 5,000 bootstrap resamples were used to estimate confidence intervals for indirect associations. Results Attitude (β = 0.564), subjective norm (β = 0.219), and perceived behavioral control (β = 0.186) were positively associated with truthful declaration intention. Non-disclosure detection certainty (NDC) was positively associated with attitude (β = 0.643) and perceived behavioral control (β = 0.588), whereas improper-use identification certainty (IIC) was negatively associated with both constructs (β = −2.175 and −2.154, respectively). Non-disclosure sanction severity was negatively associated with attitude and perceived behavioral control (β = −0.486 and −0.690, respectively), whereas improper-use sanction severity was positively associated with both constructs (β = 1.916 and 1.892, respectively). All these structural paths were statistically significant ( p < 0.001). Bootstrap analyses identified significant indirect associations with intention via both attitude and perceived behavioral control: positive for non-disclosure detection certainty and improper-use sanction severity, and negative for non-disclosure sanction severity and improper-use identification certainty. Discussion The findings highlight the value of distinguishing deterrence targets and separating detection certainty from sanction severity. These perceptions showed contrasting associations with attitude and perceived behavioral control, with corresponding model-implied indirect associations with truthful declaration intention. The results inform differentiated approaches to disclosure governance, although the conditional sanction-severity estimates require cautious interpretation.

item.title: To cheat or not to cheat? Examining undergraduate students’ use of generative AI and academic dishonesty
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become embedded in everyday university study, intensifying long-standing concerns about academic integrity now that students can obtain finished work on demand. Yet why some students cross the line into academic dishonesty—and whether teaching them to feel capable of and in control of AI protects against it—remains unclear. Framing propensity toward AI-enabled academic dishonesty as the focal educational outcome, and drawing on the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, this study used an explanatory mixed-methods design. We analyzed a cross-sectional survey of undergraduates across disciplines at several Chinese universities ( N = 1,045 after removing 115 respondents who gave the same answer to all 41 items) and semi-structured interviews with seven students, which were analyzed thematically. Academic dishonesty was common (50.1% of students scored 5 or higher on a 1–7 scale) and was most strongly associated with AI dependence ( β = 0.63), which was in turn associated with impulsivity, trust in AI, and fear of missing out; trust was also directly associated with dishonesty. Contrary to the widely held assumption that agency protects integrity, a sense of human–AI agency did not moderate the dependence–dishonesty association, and was itself positively associated with dishonesty. Habitual verification of AI output showed the complementary pattern: it did not weaken the dependence–dishonesty association, but it was associated with markedly lower dependence, and thus indirectly with less dishonesty. A latent profile analysis converged on the same account—dependence ordered the profiles on dishonesty, whereas felt agency did not order them at all—and interviewees invoked a sense of control when accounting for passing AI work off as their own. Because the survey was cross-sectional and self-reported, these are associations, not demonstrated effects. For teaching and integrity policy, they nonetheless suggest that curbing dependence and calibrating students’ trust in AI, rather than cultivating a general sense of agency, are the more promising targets.

item.title: When a feature becomes a bug: evolutionary mismatch in human–robot interaction
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As robots become increasingly integrated into everyday life, evolved psychological mechanisms originally adapted for human social interaction may shape responses to artificial agents in ways that are no longer functionally appropriate. Drawing on an evolutionary psychology framework, the present study examined how anthropomorphism, empathy, and systemizing influence decisions involving a humanoid home robot. Participants ( N = 519) completed an online experiment in which they viewed one of six robot stimuli varying in appearance (human-like, ambiguous, or robotic) and gender (female or male). They then read a scenario in which the manufacturer instructed them to reset the malfunctioning robot, thereby erasing its memories, while the robot pleaded not to be deactivated. Participants rated their willingness to deactivate the robot and the anticipated discomfort associated with doing so, and subsequently completed measures of anthropomorphism, empathy, and systemizing. Two 2 × 3 general linear models showed that stronger anthropomorphic tendencies predicted lower willingness to deactivate the robot, whereas higher systemizing predicted greater willingness. Empathy did not predict the decision itself but was associated with greater anticipated discomfort, together with anthropomorphism, while systemizing predicted lower discomfort. Contrary to our expectations, the decision to deactivate the robot did not vary as a function of its appearance. However, robot appearance influenced anticipated discomfort through interaction effects. These findings suggest that distinct evolved psychological mechanisms differentially shape behavioral and emotional responses to humanoid robots, consistent with the notion that evolutionary mismatch is at play human–robot interactions.

item.title: A Configurational Approach to Investigating the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Self‐Regulated Learning From Needs Satisfaction, Learning Environments and Perceived Affordances
item.description:
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
ABSTRACT Background Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools into self‐regulated learning (SRL) is complex and multifaceted. Configurational approaches are based on the concept that combinations (or configurations) of causally relevant factors should be connected to the desired outcome. Objectives Self‐determination theory (SDT), the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) and perceived affordances focus on basic needs, technology adoptions and technological designs, respectively. Taking a configurational approach, this study investigates how the combinations of SDT, UTAUT and perceived affordances affect SRL with AI. Methods We employed fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to uncover the complex interplay of factors that facilitate effective SRL. Data from 248 students reveal that a combination of autonomy satisfaction, relatedness satisfaction and performance expectancy is the most influential factor affecting the use of AI in SRL. Results and Conclusions Our results suggest that both innate psychological needs and external learning environments should be considered together for understanding the adoption of AI in SRL. They also further highlight the critical role of perceived affordances as mediators and moderators, enhancing the relationships between innate psychological needs and external learning environments. This integrative approach provides valuable insights into the design and implementation of AI‐supported SRL environments. We recommend designing the environments to foster autonomy and relatedness while also ensuring ease of use for learners.

item.title: Generative AI configurations across creative phases: a 2 × 2 experiment on creative performance and immediate knowledge in art and design education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in art and design education, but it remains unclear whether text-based and image-generative configurations offer different advantages across creative phases or whether sequencing them improves final outcomes. Methods In a randomized 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment, 120 art and design students (30 per condition) completed a standardized cultural-heritage chromatic reconstruction task. Participants were assigned to Text-to-Text, Text-to-Image, Image-to-Text, or Image-to-Image configurations across divergent exploration and convergent development. Expert-rated creative performance, immediate task-relevant knowledge, and human–AI interaction processes were assessed. The four primary hypothesis tests were evaluated with Holm correction. Results Text-based AI during divergence produced higher divergent creative performance than image-generative AI (mean difference = 0.823, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Image-generative AI during convergence yielded higher Aesthetic Quality at the unadjusted level (difference = 0.493, p = 0.026), but not after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.052). The hypothesized Text-to-Image sequence did not significantly outperform alternatives in Overall Creative Performance (contrast = 0.066, p = 0.671), and the factorial interaction was nonsignificant ( p = 0.541). However, Text-to-Image achieved higher baseline-adjusted immediate post-task knowledge scores (contrast = 1.478, 95% CI [1.050, 1.906], p < 0.001), without a significant cross-phase interaction ( p = 0.404). Discussion GenAI configuration effects differed across creative phases and outcomes, but phase-specific advantages did not establish a superior final creative-product sequence. Because AI modality was bundled with interaction and interface characteristics, and the knowledge assessments had limited reliability, the results do not establish isolated modality effects, durable learning, or synergistic sequencing. AI orchestration should remain a provisional, context-sensitive instructional perspective requiring further validation.

item.title: Older adults’ social responses to AI virtual humans in digital kinship contexts: associations of loneliness, perceived cues and appraisals with purchase intention
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As AI virtual humans become increasingly prominent communicative actors on short-video platforms, digital kinship content characterized by kinship-based forms of address, family narratives, caring expressions, and companionship-oriented interaction has begun to enter older adults’ everyday media use and become intertwined with commercial recommendation. Selectively drawing on the three-factor theory of anthropomorphism and integrating it with the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, this study conceptualizes loneliness as a manifestation of sociality motivation; emotional appeal, human likeness, and homophily as perceived cues and appraisals associated with elicited agent knowledge; and social presence and empathy as proximal social responses within the CASA framework. It examines older adults’ social perceptions of and emotional responses to kinship-oriented AI virtual humans and their associations with purchase intention. Using a standardized set of AI virtual human short videos representing key features of digital kinship content as stimuli, we collected valid data from 372 Chinese adults aged 65 years and older and employed partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) as parallel and complementary analytical approaches. The PLS-SEM results revealed distinct antecedent patterns for the two proximal responses. Emotional appeal showed the strongest association with social presence, whereas homophily was more strongly associated with empathy than with social presence. Human likeness was significantly associated only with social presence, while loneliness was positively associated with both responses. Empathy showed a stronger association with purchase intention than social presence, and all indirect associations were significant except the pathway from human likeness through empathy. The fsQCA results further showed that the combination of emotional appeal and empathy constituted the most stable configuration associated with high purchase intention, whereas loneliness emerged as a core condition only when homophily was also present. This study provides empirical evidence for understanding perceptions of social presence and empathy in later-life human–AI relational perception and offers practical implications for the governance of kinship-oriented AI commercial content and the protection of older consumers.

item.title: Artificial intelligence sycophancy, epistemic calibration, and verification intentions in first-year aerospace engineering students’ evaluation of research proposals
item.description:
Thinking Skills and Creativity
AI-generated responses may shape students’ judgements through both their informational content and their interpersonal style. This study examined whether conversational praise and epistemic stance were associated with differences in first-year students’ evaluations of research proposals and their self-reported need to verify claims of novelty. Participants were 120 first-year Aerospace Engineering students at a Spanish university, randomly assigned to one of four conditions in a 2 × 2 between-participants design crossing conversational tone (praising vs. neutral) with epistemic stance (unsupported validation vs. evidence-oriented calibrated assessment). Each participant reviewed the same four aerospace topics under one assigned condition and then completed one global evaluation. Factorial analyses showed significant effects of tone and epistemic stance on perceived novelty and perceived need to verify; the largest effect was the stance effect on need to verify, 𝐹 ⁡ ( 1 1 1 6 ) = 6 7 . 9 0 , 𝑝 < . 0 0 1 , 𝜂 2 𝑝 = . 3 6 9 . Epistemic stance was also associated with differences in choice intention, perceived publication probability, and detection of sycophancy, while tone showed the clearest independent effect on trust in AI. Final decisions differed across conditions: direct acceptance was 63.3% under praising + validation and 10.0% under neutral + calibrated assessment, whereas choosing to search the literature was 10.0% and 46.7%, respectively. A directed content analysis of the open-ended responses was descriptively consistent with this pattern: systematic verification strategies and requests for evidential support were more frequent under calibrated assessment than under validation. Because calibrated responses explicitly introduced prior-work and verification cues, these effects should be interpreted as consequences of the broader contrast between unsupported validation and evidence-oriented calibration, not as a pure effect of disagreement. The study measures verification intention rather than observed verification behaviour or general critical-thinking ability.

item.title: Cognitive Regulation in Generative AI Use: A Network Study of Anxiety and Dependence Among Foreign Language Majors
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
Anxiety accompanying students’ reliance on generative AI has been linked to appraisals of their own competence and to comparison with peers, two complementary routes usually modeled separately. This study asked which nodes retain conditional associations with AI-related anxiety and dependence when both routes are modeled together. Survey responses from 283 foreign language majors formed a 17-node regularized partial correlation network, supplemented by written responses from 21 students. Social-comparison anxiety was the only anxiety node connected with dependence (partial r = 0.177, 95% bootstrap interval [0.077, 0.280]); exploratory facet analyses located it mainly in fear of falling behind or missing out, less consistently in peer competence pressure, and not in upward comparison. The three measured self-appraisal nodes, which assessed broad confidence, were unrelated to anxiety conditionally and at the zero-order level. The dependence association was modest, had no resolved direction, and was retained only in the fourth-year network; no cohort difference was established, and study year was confounded with collection period. Written responses did not corroborate this association but revealed integrity boundaries, guilt, and redefined language competence, which the survey omitted. The findings identify candidate correlates of reliance that require replication in independent samples, and content missing from AI anxiety instruments.

item.title: When thanks have nowhere to go: emotional indebtedness in the age of service robots
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction When hotel service robots deliver meaningful service, customers may experience emotional indebtedness—a moral-emotional state arising from perceived obligation without a clear target for reciprocity. This study examines how social (social presence, enjoyment) and nonsocial (novelty, performance) attributes of service robots influence emotional indebtedness and subsequent brand loyalty. Methods Survey data were collected from 462 hotel guests in China with direct service robot experience. Structural equation modeling (SEM) with maximum likelihood estimation was employed, incorporating second-order latent constructs and multi-group analysis by anthropomorphism level. Results Social attributes significantly increased emotional indebtedness, whereas nonsocial attributes either reduced or failed to elicit such responses. Emotional indebtedness positively predicted brand loyalty. Multi-group analyses revealed that the effect of social attributes on emotional indebtedness was invariant across anthropomorphism levels, whereas anthropomorphism moderated the relationship between nonsocial attributes and emotional indebtedness and the conversion of indebtedness into brand loyalty. Discussion These findings extend social exchange theory to robot-mediated hospitality services, demonstrating that customers’ moral-emotional responses depend more on how robot interactions are socially interpreted than on functional performance alone. Anthropomorphism functions as a selective boundary condition rather than a uniform amplifier of emotional engagement.

item.title: sEMG-Integrated AR Prediction and Adaptive Impedance Control for Physical Human–Robot Interaction with BLF Safety Constraints
item.description:
International Journal of Social Robotics
